bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

A function is a machine. Put a number in the top, and a number comes out of the bottom. $f(x) = 2x + 3$ is the machine that doubles whatever you feed it and then adds 3.

A **composite** function is two machines bolted together: the output of the first is poured straight into the second. An **inverse** function is the machine running backwards — it undoes what the original did.

## What is actually going on

$(f \circ g)(x)$ means $f(g(x))$: $g$ runs **first**, then $f$. The order matters, and reading it right to left is what keeps people out of trouble.

The inverse $f^{-1}$ answers 'what input would have produced this output?'. To find it, write $y = f(x)$, swap the roles of $x$ and $y$, and solve. If $f$ doubles and adds 3, then $f^{-1}$ subtracts 3 and halves — the same steps, reversed and undone.

workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Inside first: $g(6) = 6 - 4 = 2$.

Then feed that into $f$: $f(2) = 3(2) + 1 = 7$.

So $(f \circ g)(6) = 7$.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Note $(g \circ f)(6) = g(19) = 15$, a completely different answer. Order is not optional.

workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
We want the input that gives an output of 11.

$4x - 5 = 11$, so $4x = 16$ and $x = 4$.

So $f^{-1}(11) = 4$. Check: $f(4) = 16 - 5 = 11$.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: The general inverse is $f^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{y + 5}{4}$: add 5, then divide by 4 — undoing the original steps in reverse order.

formulaCards.title: Composition
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$ — apply $g$ first. In general $f \circ g \neq g \circ f$.

formulaCards.title: Inverse
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $f^{-1}$ satisfies $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$. Find it by setting $y = f(x)$ and solving for $x$.

commonTraps: Applying the outer function first. In $f(g(x))$, $g$ goes first.
Reading $f^{-1}(x)$ as $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The superscript $-1$ means inverse, not reciprocal.
Assuming every function has an inverse. It needs each output to come from exactly one input.
